mainTopic: How an act can forbid another's property or an exchange for עבודה זרה (including חליפי חליפין and שביעית), and why God does not destroy objects of idol worship
overview: The amud opens by explaining how someone who slaughters another person's animal for עבודה זרה can forbid it, even though a person cannot forbid what is not his. The proof is the Temple כלים of אחז: because a real act of worship was done with them, they became forbidden. רבי יוחנן adds two cases where an act forbids things that bowing alone does not: digging pits in the ground, and trading animals for an idol. רבין then reports a מחלוקת about whether an exchange of an exchange (חליפי חליפין) is also forbidden. Each side explains its verse, and the debate turns on whether שני כתובין הבאין כאחד teach other cases, with שביעית as the example of status passing along a chain of purchases. A new משנה follows, telling how the elders in Rome explained why God does not destroy idols: the world needs the sun and moon, and He will not destroy His world because of fools. The גמרא adds that the world follows its normal course and sinners will be judged later. It ends with רבן גמליאל's parables answering a philosopher, and his supporting פסוק comes on the next amud.

steps.title: A source from the Temple vessels of King Ahaz
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings the כלים that אחז used for idol worship as a source. Those כלים became forbidden: they were put away and new ones were made holy in their place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn it from the vessels. The פסוק says: 'And all the vessels which King אחז cast away in his reign, in his treachery, we have prepared and sanctified.' And the Master explained: 'we have prepared' means we put them away (hid them), and 'sanctified' means we sanctified other vessels in their place.
steps.whatsHappening: Earlier attempts did not work, so the גמרא offers a new source: the Temple vessels that אחז misused. They became forbidden for Temple use.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק, as the Master explains it, shows that אחז's vessels could no longer be used. They had to be hidden away and replaced. So something that did not belong to אחז became forbidden through his idol worship, which is just what our case needs.

keyTerms.meaning: Vessels or utensils (here, the Temple vessels)
Cast away, defiled through misuse
We put them away (hid them so they would not be used)
We made holy (dedicated new vessels)
In their place

phrases.english: But rather, from vessels,
as it is written:
"And all the vessels
which King Ahaz cast away
in his reign, in his treachery,
we have prepared and sanctified,"
phrases.notes: דברי הימים ב 29:19

phrases.english: And the Master said:
"We have prepared" means that we put them away,
"and sanctified" means that we sanctified other vessels in their place,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֶלָּא מִכֵּלִים, דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a new source after earlier attempts (on the previous part of the daf) were rejected.
steps.raayaObject: That a person can make forbidden something that does not belong to him, like slaughtering another's animal for עבודה זרה
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים ב 29:19, as explained by the Master: אחז's vessels were put away and replaced

steps.title: But a person cannot forbid what is not his
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא points out the problem: the vessels belonged to the הקדש, not to אחז. So how did he forbid them?
steps.simpleTranslation: But a person cannot make forbidden something that is not his!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises the obvious difficulty with the vessels. It is the very same problem we started with, and it sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a general rule that a person cannot forbid property that is not his. אחז did not own the Temple vessels. So the vessels case is just as puzzling as the animal case, and the גמרא must explain how they became forbidden.

keyTerms.term: אֵין אָדָם אוֹסֵר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ
keyTerms.meaning: A person cannot make forbidden something that is not his

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an attack that throws out the vessels source. It sharpens the question so that the answer in the next step explains both the vessels and the animal.

phrases.english: But a person does not
make forbidden something that is not his!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אֵין אָדָם אוֹסֵר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ שֶׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the vessels in step 1 could have become forbidden at all.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fact that אחז's vessels became forbidden (step 1)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person cannot forbid what he does not own, and אחז did not own the Temple vessels.

steps.title: Doing an act on an item forbids it, so the animal is forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: Since אחז did a real act of worship with the vessels, they became forbidden. In the same way, someone who slaughters another person's animal for עבודה זרה forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, since he did an act with them, they became forbidden. Here too, since he did an act with the animal, he forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that an actual act of worship forbids an item even if it belongs to someone else. It then applies this to our case of the animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Simply declaring or bowing cannot forbid someone else's property. A physical act of worship (מעשה) is different and does forbid it. Slaughtering an animal is such an act, so the other person's animal becomes forbidden, just like אחז's vessels.

keyTerms.meaning: He did an act with them (a physical act of worship)
They became forbidden
Here too (applying the same idea to our case)

steps.whatToRemember: A person cannot forbid what is not his by words alone. A real act of worship (מעשה), like using the vessels or slaughtering the animal, does forbid it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives the reason behind the rule that שוחט בהמת חבירו לעבודה זרה makes the animal forbidden. It also sets up the next teachings, where an act forbids things that bowing does not.

phrases.english: Rather, since he performed an act with them,
phrases.notes: He means אחז actually used the vessels for idol worship, not just bowed to them.

phrases.english: they became forbidden;
here too,
since he performed an act with it,
phrases.notes: "It" is the other person's animal, which he slaughtered for idol worship.

phrases.english: he made it forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, כֵּיוָן דַּעֲבַד בְּהוּ מַעֲשֶׂה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the difficulty of step 2 and uses the vessels source for the animal case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: words cannot forbid another's property, but a physical act can
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A person can never forbid something that is not his.
steps.terutzMaskana: A real act of worship forbids the item even if it belongs to someone else, so the slaughtered animal is forbidden.

steps.title: Digging in the ground for idol worship forbids it
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports in the name of רבי יוחנן: bowing to the ground does not forbid it, but digging pits, ditches, and caves in it for idol worship does.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said that רבי יוחנן says: even though the חכמים said that one who bows to the ground does not forbid it, if he dug pits, ditches, and caves in it, he forbade it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching begins. It reports that the ground, which normally cannot become forbidden through bowing, does become forbidden if someone digs in it for idol worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קרקע עולם, ground that is still attached, normally cannot become forbidden by bowing to it. Digging pits and caves for the idol is a physical act done to the ground itself, and that changes the result. This matches the idea in step 3 that a real act forbids where bowing alone does not.

keyTerms.meaning: When he came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)
One who bows down (to worship)
The natural ground, still attached to the earth
Pits, ditches, and caves

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came,
he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
Even though they said
one who bows to the ground
does not make it forbidden,
if he dug pits, ditches, and caves in it,
he made it forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new report that fits the idea of step 3: an act forbids where bowing does not.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Ground is not forbidden by bowing to it, but digging pits, ditches, and caves in it for idol worship forbids it.

steps.title: Trading animals for an idol forbids them
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר יהודה reports in the name of רבי יוחנן: bowing to animals does not forbid them, but using them as payment in exchange for עבודה זרה does.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב שמואל בר יהודה came, he said that רבי יוחנן says: even though the חכמים said that one who bows to animals does not forbid them, if he made them an exchange for an object of עבודה זרה, he forbade them.
steps.whatsHappening: A second report from רבי יוחנן, following the same pattern as step 4. Animals are not forbidden by being bowed to, but they are forbidden if traded for an idol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Living animals do not become forbidden just because someone bowed to them. If the animal is given in exchange for an object of עבודה זרה, it takes on the forbidden status of the idol as its חליפין. Again, a real action does what bowing alone cannot.

keyTerms.meaning: Living animals
An exchange, something traded for something else
Idol worship, or an object of idol worship

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came,
he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
Even though they said
one who bows to animals
does not make them forbidden,
if he made them an exchange for idol worship,
he made them forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יְהוּדָה, אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel teaching to step 4, this time about animals instead of ground.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals are not forbidden by bowing to them, but if traded in exchange for an object of עבודה זרה they become forbidden.

steps.title: Is an exchange of an exchange also forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: רבין reports a מחלוקת between רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי and the רבנן. One holds that only the first exchange is forbidden. The other holds that even an exchange of the exchange is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבין came, he said: רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי and the רבנן disagree about this. One says: the exchange is forbidden, but the exchange of the exchange is permitted. And one says: even the exchange of the exchange is also forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: Building on step 5's rule about חליפין, רבין reports a disagreement about how far the prohibition goes when items are traded again and again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that an item traded directly for עבודה זרה is forbidden. They disagree about the next trade, when that forbidden item is itself traded for something else. One view says the prohibition stops after the first exchange. The other says it carries on even to the second exchange. The גמרא does not say which side holds which view.

keyTerms.meaning: They disagree about it
One says
An exchange of an exchange (a second trade)
Permitted

steps.whatToRemember: An item traded for עבודה זרה is forbidden. Whether a second trade (חליפי חליפין) is also forbidden is a מחלוקת between רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי and the רבנן.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא does not tell us here which opinion belongs to רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי and which to the רבנן. It only says 'one says' and 'one says'.

phrases.english: When Ravin came, he said:
They disagree about it,
phrases.notes: "It" is the rule about items traded for idol worship, from the step before.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בַּר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis:
One says: the exchange is forbidden,
but the exchange of the exchange is permitted,
and one says:
even the exchange of the exchange is also forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר: פְּלִיגוּ בַּהּ רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בַּר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי וְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands on the חליפין rule of step 5 by asking whether a second trade is also forbidden.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A מחלוקת: one view holds only the first exchange is forbidden, and the other holds even the exchange of the exchange is forbidden.

steps.title: What is the source for forbidding a second exchange?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason of the opinion from Step 6 that says even an exchange of an exchange is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of the one who says that an exchange of an exchange is forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind the stricter opinion in the מחלוקת from Step 6. This question sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 6 we only heard the two opinions, not their reasons. Now the גמרא wants to know what verse the strict side relies on to forbid even the second exchange.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
An exchange of an exchange: something traded for an item that was itself traded for the idol
The one who says (a particular opinion)

phrases.english: What is the reason of the one who says
that an exchange of an exchange is forbidden?
phrases.notes: This goes back to the מחלוקת in Step 6 between רבי ישמעאל בר רבי יוסי and the רבנן.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא דְּמַאן דְּאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the verse behind the strict opinion in the מחלוקת of Step 6.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The verse that teaches that חליפי חליפין of עבודה זרה are forbidden.

steps.title: Anything you get from the idol is like it
steps.stepSummary: The strict side learns from 'והיית חרם כמהו' that anything you get from the idol is just as forbidden as the idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says: 'And you will become accursed like it.' Anything you bring into being from it is just like it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the strict side's source. The verse says 'והיית חרם כמהו', and he reads it as 'anything you produce from it is like it'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'והיית' (you will become) is read as connected to 'מְהַיֶּה' (to bring into being). So whatever comes into your hands from the idol, through any number of trades, is forbidden 'like it'. That is why even the second exchange is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: Accursed, forbidden like a banned object
Brings into being, produces
Like it

phrases.english: The verse says: 'And you will become accursed like it,'
phrases.notes: דברים 7:26.

phrases.english: anything that you bring into being from it
phrases.notes: The word 'וְהָיִיתָ' is being read like 'מְהַיֶּה', meaning whatever you get out of the idol.

phrases.english: is just like it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: ״וְהָיִיתָ חֵרֶם כָּמֹהוּ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse 'והיית חרם כמהו' teaches that everything gained from the idol, even through further exchanges, is forbidden like it.

steps.title: The other side: only 'it' is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The lenient side learns from the word 'הוא' that only the idol (and its direct exchange) is forbidden, not an exchange of an exchange.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one: the verse says 'it.' 'It' is forbidden, but not an exchange of an exchange.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the source of the lenient side. He points to the word 'הוא' (it) in the same verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'הוא' limits the rule. It tells us the ban stays with the idol itself and does not keep spreading down a chain of trades. So the second exchange is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)
It: a word read as limiting the rule

phrases.english: And the other one: the verse says 'it' —
phrases.notes: This is from the end of the same פסוק: 'כִּי חֵרֶם הוּא', 'for it is accursed'.

phrases.english: 'it,' and not an exchange of an exchange.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, אָמַר קְרָא: ״הוּא״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite side's source from the same verse.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word 'הוא' limits the ban to the idol itself, so חליפי חליפין are permitted.

steps.title: The strict side uses 'הוא' for ערלה and כלאי הכרם
steps.stepSummary: The strict side needs the word 'הוא' for something else: to teach that money from selling ערלה or כלאי הכרם is not forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? He needs that word to exclude ערלה and כלאי הכרם: if someone sold them and used the money to marry a woman, she is married.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the strict side does with the word 'הוא', and answers that he uses it for a different lesson. 'הוא' teaches that only עבודה זרה passes its ban onto money, not ערלה or כלאי הכרם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each side must explain the word the other side relies on. For the strict side, 'הוא' means only עבודה זרה transfers its ban to what you get for it. So money from selling ערלה or כלאי הכרם is permitted, and a קידושין done with that money works.

keyTerms.meaning: He needs it (for another teaching)
To exclude
Fruit of a tree in its first three years, forbidden to benefit from
Mixed crops planted in a vineyard, forbidden to benefit from
Betrothed a woman (קידושין)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'וְאִידַּךְ' means the strict side, not the same person as in Step 9. Each 'ואידך' switches to whichever side has not yet been asked about.

phrases.english: And the other one? He needs that
phrases.notes: Now we are asking the strict side what he does with the word 'הוּא'.

phrases.english: to exclude ערלה and כלאי הכרם,
that if he sold them and betrothed a woman with their money, she is betrothed.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, הָהוּא מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the strict side reads the lenient side's word 'הוא', and answers.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The lenient side reads 'הוא' as limiting the ban to the idol and not its exchange of an exchange. So what does the strict side do with that word?
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redirecting the verse to a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'הוא' must be limiting the chain of exchanges.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'הוא' limits the ban to עבודה זרה, excluding money from ערלה and כלאי הכרם.

steps.title: No verse needed: שני כתובין הבאין כאחד
steps.stepSummary: The lenient side says ערלה and כלאי הכרם need no special verse, because עבודה זרה and שביעית are two verses teaching the same rule, and such verses do not teach other cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one? ערלה and כלאי הכרם do not need an exclusion. עבודה זרה and שביעית are two verses that come as one, and any two verses that come as one do not teach about other cases.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the lenient side knows ערלה money is permitted without the word 'הוא'. He answers that a general rule already teaches it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two areas of law, עבודה זרה and שביעית, both say the ban moves onto the money. When the תורה repeats the same rule in two places, it shows the rule belongs only to those cases. So ערלה and כלאי הכרם are permitted automatically, and 'הוא' is free to limit the chain of exchanges.

keyTerms.meaning: An exclusion taught from a verse
The seventh year (שמיטה) and its produce
Two verses that teach the same rule
They do not teach (about other cases)

steps.whatToRemember: When the same rule appears in two separate places (שני כתובין הבאין כאחד), we do not apply it to other cases. That is why ערלה money is permitted even without a special verse.

phrases.english: And the other one? ערלה and כלאי הכרם
phrases.notes: Now we are back to the lenient side: how does he know ערלה money is permitted?

phrases.english: do not need an exclusion,
because עבודה זרה and שביעית are
two verses that come as one,
and any two verses that come as one
do not teach about other cases.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, עׇרְלָה וְכִלְאֵי הַכֶּרֶם לָא צְרִיכִי מִיעוּטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns Step 10's point back on the lenient side and shows he needs no verse for ערלה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'הוא' is used to limit exchanges, where does he learn that ערלה and כלאי הכרם money is permitted?
steps.terutzResolutionType: A general rule makes the extra verse unnecessary
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A verse is needed to exclude ערלה and כלאי הכרם.
steps.terutzMaskana: שני כתובין הבאין כאחד אין מלמדין, so ערלה and כלאי הכרם are excluded automatically.

steps.title: The two verses: עבודה זרה and שביעית
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא identifies the two verses: עבודה זרה's verse was already given, and שביעית's comes from comparing it to קודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: עבודה זרה: what we said. שביעית: as it is written, 'For it is יובל, it shall be holy for you.' Just as קודש passes onto its money and the money is forbidden, so too שביעית passes onto its money and the money is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows which two verses it meant in Step 11. For שביעית, it compares the produce to קודש, which passes its status onto the money paid for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse calls the year 'קודש'. Just as holy property moves its holiness onto the money it is redeemed with, שביעית produce moves its status onto its money. Together with עבודה זרה, these are the two verses teaching the same rule.

keyTerms.meaning: What we already said
The fiftieth (Jubilee) year
Holy property
Catches its money: passes its status onto the money paid for it

phrases.english: עבודה זרה: what we already said,
שביעית: as it is written:
'For it is a Jubilee; it shall be holy for you,'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:12.

phrases.aramaic: מָה קֹדֶשׁ תּוֹפֵס אֶת דָּמָיו וְאָסוּר,
phrases.english: just as holy property passes onto its money, and the money is forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: אַף שְׁבִיעִית תּוֹפֶסֶת אֶת דָּמֶיהָ וַאֲסוּרָה.
phrases.english: so too, שביעית passes onto its money, and the money is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה — הָא דַּאֲמַרַן, שְׁבִיעִית — דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the two verses that Step 11 called שני כתובין הבאין כאחד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both עבודה זרה and שביעית pass their ban onto the money paid for them; for שביעית this is learned by comparing it to קודש.

steps.title: If שביעית is like קודש, does the fruit lose its status?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the comparison of שביעית to קודש. When קודש is redeemed, the money becomes holy and the item becomes ordinary. So maybe שביעית fruit also becomes ordinary once it is exchanged.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you compare them: just as קודש passes its holiness onto the money and itself becomes ordinary, maybe שביעית fruit also passes its status onto the money and itself becomes ordinary!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the comparison to קודש from the last step. If the comparison is complete, it seems to lead to a lenient result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With קודש, the holiness moves over to the redemption money, and the original item is no longer holy. If שביעית is compared to קודש in every way, the fruit itself should become permitted after the exchange. That would be a problem, so the גמרא needs to limit the comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: Consecrated property that belongs to the בית המקדש
Takes hold of its money, meaning its status passes onto the money paid for it
Goes out to ordinary, non-holy status
The seventh year, whose produce has special holiness

phrases.aramaic: אִי מָה קֹדֶשׁ תּוֹפֵס אֶת דָּמָיו
phrases.english: If so, just as consecrated property takes hold of its money
and itself goes out to ordinary status,
so too, שביעית produce should take hold of its money
and itself go out to ordinary status!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי מָה קֹדֶשׁ תּוֹפֵס אֶת דָּמָיו

steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison of שביעית to קודש
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A full comparison would mean the fruit loses its status once exchanged, just like redeemed קודש does.

steps.title: The word 'תִּהְיֶה' keeps the fruit forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The verse says 'תִּהְיֶה' ('it shall be'). This teaches that שביעית fruit stays in its status even after it is exchanged.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says 'it shall be.' It stays as it is.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with one word from the פסוק. The fruit keeps its status even though the money also takes it on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the comparison to קודש is limited. Like קודש, the status of שביעית passes onto the money. Unlike קודש, the original fruit does not become ordinary.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse teaches
'It shall be', a word in the פסוק about שביעית
It shall remain in its state

phrases.english: The verse says: "It shall be",
phrases.notes: ויקרא 25:12

phrases.english: it shall remain in its state.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the comparison by using an extra word in the verse
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שביעית fruit becomes ordinary once exchanged, like קודש.
steps.terutzMaskana: The money takes on the שביעית status, and the fruit itself also stays forbidden.

steps.title: How the שביעית status moves along a chain of purchases
steps.stepSummary: A worked example: fruit buys meat, meat buys fish, fish buys wine, wine buys oil. Each new item takes on the status and the one before it lets go. The original fruit always stays forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: How does this work? If he bought meat with שביעית fruit, both must be removed in the שביעית time. If he then bought fish with the meat, the meat goes out and the fish come in. With the fish he bought wine: the fish go out and the wine comes in. With the wine he bought oil: the wine goes out and the oil comes in. So what is the rule? Each newest item is caught with the שביעית status, and the fruit itself stays forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an example to show exactly how the rule of 'תִּהְיֶה' plays out in real purchases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only two things carry the status at any moment: the original fruit and the newest item bought. The items in the middle become ordinary as soon as they are traded for the next thing. This shows that שביעית does carry over to an exchange of an exchange.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? How does this work?
Must be removed (the duty of ביעור for שביעית produce)
Each newest item in the chain
Is caught, meaning it takes on the status

steps.whatToRemember: With שביעית, the status jumps to each new item bought, the middle items drop it, and the original fruit keeps its שביעית status.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the meat, fish and wine all stay forbidden. Only the original fruit and the newest item are forbidden at any time.

phrases.english: How so?
If he bought meat with שביעית fruit,
both these and those must be removed in the שביעית time,
phrases.notes: 'These and those' are the meat and the fruit. Both now carry the שביעית status.

phrases.english: if he bought fish with the meat,
the meat goes out and the fish come in,
phrases.notes: 'Goes out' means it loses the status, and 'come in' means they take it on.

phrases.english: with the fish he bought wine,
the fish go out and the wine comes in,
with the wine he bought oil,
the wine goes out and the oil comes in,
So what is the rule?
each newest item is caught with the שביעית status,
and the fruit itself stays forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא כֵּיצַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows in practice how the rule from step 14 works.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The שביעית status passes to each newest item bought, the middle items become ordinary, and the original fruit stays forbidden.

steps.title: The strict side: two matching verses do teach, so 'הוא' is needed
steps.stepSummary: The strict side answers the lenient side from step 11. He holds that two verses teaching the same rule do teach other cases. So without 'הוא', we would have applied the rule to ערלה and כלאי הכרם.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other one holds that two verses that come as one do teach other cases. So 'it' was needed to leave them out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the strict side's answer to the lenient side's argument from step 11, and this closes the debate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lenient side said עבודה זרה and שביעית are two verses that teach the same rule, so they cannot be used for other cases, and 'הוא' is free to teach his own point. The strict side disagrees about that general principle: he holds that such verses do teach other cases. Without 'הוא', ערלה and כלאי הכרם would also forbid their exchange money, so the word is needed to exclude them.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one, meaning the other side of the debate
Two verses that teach the same rule
They do teach, meaning the rule spreads to other cases
To exclude them

steps.whatToRemember: The whole debate comes down to whether two verses teaching the same rule can teach other cases. That decides what the word 'הוא' is needed for.
steps.confusionAlert: 'וְאִידַּךְ' here is the strict side, the one who says even an exchange of an exchange is forbidden. He is not the lenient side from step 11.

phrases.english: And the other one holds:
phrases.notes: This is the strict side from step 10, answering the point made in step 11.

phrases.english: two verses that come as one do teach other cases,
so "it" was needed to exclude them.
phrases.notes: 'Them' means ערלה and כלאי הכרם.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, קָסָבַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the strict side and answers the argument from step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the two sides disagree about a general rule for reading verses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Two verses teaching the same rule cannot teach other cases, so 'הוא' is free for another lesson.
steps.terutzMaskana: The strict side holds that such verses do teach, so 'הוא' is needed to exclude ערלה and כלאי הכרם.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the whole argument over 'הוא' depends on a basic disagreement about how verses teach.

steps.title: Why God does not wipe out עבודה זרה
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה. The elders in Rome were asked why God does not destroy idols if He hates idol worship. They answered that people worship the sun, moon and stars, and God will not destroy His world because of fools.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked the elders in Rome: if God does not want עבודה זרה, why doesn't He destroy it? They answered: if people worshipped only things the world does not need, He would destroy them. But they worship the sun, the moon, the stars and the constellations. Should He destroy His world because of fools?!
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It records a question the elders were asked in Rome and the answer they gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes that God could simply remove every idol. The answer explains that many idols are basic parts of creation that the world needs. Destroying them would harm everyone just because of the mistake of a few foolish people.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה, the start of a new משנה
The elders, meaning the חכמים
Destroys it, gets rid of it
Constellations
Fools

steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה opens a new discussion about why God lets objects of עבודה זרה keep existing. The גמרא and the stories that follow build on its answer.

phrases.english: משנה:
They asked the elders in Rome:
If He does not want idol worship,
why doesn't He destroy it?
They said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אִילּוּ לְדָבָר שֶׁאֵין צוֹרֶךְ לָעוֹלָם בּוֹ
phrases.english: If it were a thing the world has no need for
that they were worshipping, He would destroy it,
but they worship the sun and the moon
and the stars and the constellations,
should He destroy His world because of the fools?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the previous discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God does not destroy objects of idol worship that the world needs, such as the sun and the moon, because of the foolishness of those who worship them.

steps.title: Then let God destroy only the useless idols
steps.stepSummary: The questioners push back on the elders: if God spares idols only because the world needs them, let Him destroy the useless ones and leave the needed ones.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to them: If so, let Him destroy the things the world has no need for, and leave the things the world does need!
steps.whatsHappening: The questioners challenge the elders' answer from step 17. They say God could at least wipe out the idols the world does not need.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The elders said God will not destroy the sun, moon and stars because the world needs them. The questioners agree with that point but ask why the useless idols, like statues of wood and stone, are not destroyed. They are trying to show that the elders' answer only covers some idols.

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if that is your reasoning
Let Him destroy
Need; use
Let Him leave alone

phrases.english: They said to them: If so,

phrases.aramaic: יְאַבֵּד דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין צוֹרֶךְ לָעוֹלָם בּוֹ,
phrases.english: let Him destroy a thing the world has no need for,
and leave a thing the world does need!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן: אִם כֵּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the elders' answer in step 17 by suggesting a partial destruction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The elders' claim that God does not destroy idols because the world needs them.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reason only protects useful objects. Useless idols could still be destroyed, so the answer seems incomplete.

steps.title: Destroying some idols would make the others look real
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that destroying only the useless idols would strengthen people who worship the sun and moon, since they would claim their gods survived.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to them: Then we would be strengthening the worshippers of these, who would say: Know that these are gods, since they were not destroyed.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer the challenge from step 18. Destroying only some idols would backfire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If God destroyed the statues but left the sun and moon, the sun and moon worshippers would use this as proof. They would say their gods are real because they survived. So a partial destruction would make עבודה זרה stronger, not weaker.

keyTerms.meaning: Strengthening the hands of; supporting
Gods
Were destroyed; were done away with

steps.whatToRemember: God does not destroy idols because the world needs some of them, and destroying only the useless ones would make the rest look like real gods.

phrases.english: They said to them: Then we too would be strengthening
the hands of the worshippers of these,
phrases.notes: 'These' means the things the world needs, like the sun and moon, which would be left standing.

phrases.english: who would say: Know that these are gods,
since they were not destroyed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לָהֶן: אַף אָנוּ מַחֲזִיקִין יְדֵי עוֹבְדֵיהֶן שֶׁל אֵלּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows that the suggested alternative would cause harm.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: God could destroy just the useless idols with no downside.
steps.terutzMaskana: A partial destruction would 'prove' to idol worshippers that the surviving objects are real gods.

steps.title: The philosophers ask why God does not destroy idol worship
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: philosophers asked the elders in Rome why God does not end עבודה זרה if He does not want it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: Philosophers asked the elders in Rome: If your God does not want idol worship, why does He not destroy it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins and quotes a ברייתא that tells the same story as the משנה. This step sets up the question that the elders will answer next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is the same one the משנה asked. The ברייתא adds who asked (philosophers), and its answer in the next step adds a new principle that the משנה did not state.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
Philosophers
Elders; Sages
Destroys it; ends it

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
Philosophers asked the elders in Rome:

phrases.aramaic: אִם אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֵין רְצוֹנוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
phrases.english: If your God does not want idol worship,
why does He not destroy it?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: שָׁאֲלוּ פִלוֹסוֹפִין אֶת הַזְּקֵנִים בְּרוֹמִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא with a ברייתא that parallels the משנה from step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why God allows עבודה זרה to continue if He is against it.

steps.title: The world follows its course, and fools will be judged
steps.stepSummary: The elders answer that God would destroy useless idols, but people also worship the sun, moon and stars. God will not ruin the world for fools. The world runs normally, and the sinners will be judged later.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to them: If people worshipped only things the world does not need, He would destroy them. But they worship the sun, the moon, the stars and the constellations. Should He destroy the world because of fools? Rather, the world follows its normal course, and the fools who sinned will face judgment in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The elders answer the philosophers' question. They add a big principle: God lets the world run normally and punishes sinners later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first part repeats the משנה: the world needs the sun and moon, so God will not destroy them. The new part is 'עולם כמנהגו נוהג': nature keeps working even when people misuse it. Justice is not skipped; it is delayed until the future judgment.

keyTerms.meaning: The sun
The moon
Constellations
Fools
The world follows its normal course
To face judgment; to be held accountable

steps.whyThisMatters: The principle 'עולם כמנהגו נוהג' explains why nature does not stop for sin. The next two examples are built on it.

phrases.english: They said to them: If, to a thing

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין הָעוֹלָם צוֹרֶךְ לוֹ הָיוּ עוֹבְדִין,
phrases.english: that the world has no need for, they were worshipping,
then He would destroy it.
But they worship the sun and the moon
and the stars and the constellations.
Should He destroy the world because of the fools?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the philosophers' question from step 20.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God does not destroy the needed parts of creation because of fools. The world runs normally, and sinners will be judged in the future.

steps.title: Stolen wheat still grows
steps.stepSummary: A second example of the same idea: stolen wheat that is planted should not grow by right, but it does, because the world follows its course. The thief will be judged.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another matter: Someone stole a סאה of wheat and went and planted it in the ground. By right it should not grow. But the world keeps following its normal course, and the fools who did wrong will face judgment in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives another example of 'the world follows its course.' Even stolen seeds grow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strict justice says the stolen wheat should not sprout. But the ground works the same way for everyone, honest or not. The thief is not let off; his punishment simply comes later.

keyTerms.meaning: Another matter; another example
Stole; robbed
A סאה, a measure of volume
By right; strict justice says

phrases.english: By right it should not grow,
but the world keeps following its normal course,

phrases.aramaic: וְשׁוֹטִים שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ עֲתִידִין לִיתֵּן אֶת הַדִּין.
phrases.english: and the fools who did wrong will face judgment in the future.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּבָר אַחֵר: הֲרֵי שֶׁגָּזַל סְאָה שֶׁל חִטִּים

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Nature works normally even with stolen seeds. The thief will be punished in the future.

steps.title: A forbidden relationship can still produce a child
steps.stepSummary: A third example: a woman in a forbidden relationship should not become pregnant by right, but she can, because the world follows its course. The sinners will be judged.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another matter: Someone had relations with another man's wife. By right she should not become pregnant. But the world keeps following its normal course, and the fools who did wrong will face judgment in the future.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a final example of the same principle, this time about a serious sin between people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Strict justice says a child should not come from such a sin. But nature does not stop working because people misuse it. This closes the ברייתא with three cases that make one point: sinners are not spared, but their judgment comes later.

keyTerms.meaning: Had relations with
Another man's wife
She becomes pregnant

steps.whatToRemember: Three examples (idols, stolen wheat, adultery) teach one idea: עולם כמנהגו נוהג. Nature does not stop for sin, and the sinners will face judgment in the future.
steps.confusionAlert: The fact that nature keeps working does not mean God approves of the sin. The ברייתא says clearly that the sinners will still be judged.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: sinners force God to finish their work
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says in God's name that the wicked misuse His 'coin' as if it were ownerless, and on top of that they make Him 'stamp' the result against His will.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what ריש לקיש said: הקדוש ברוך הוא said: It is not enough for the wicked that they use My coin as if it were public property. They also trouble Me and make Me put My stamp on it against My will.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a saying of ריש לקיש that matches the last example, the woman in a forbidden relationship who still becomes pregnant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Creating a child is like God's 'coin stamp', and adulterers use it without permission. Even so, God still forms the baby, which is His 'stamp' on their act. This is the same idea as 'the world follows its course': nature keeps working, and the sinners will be judged later.

Against My will

steps.title: A philosopher asks why God punishes the worshippers but not the idol

steps.simpleTranslation: A certain philosopher asked רבן גמליאל: It is written in your תורה, 'For ה׳ your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.' Why is He jealous of the idol's worshippers but not jealous of the idol itself?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. A philosopher challenges רבן גמליאל with a question based on a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If God is 'jealous' about idolatry, the philosopher expects Him to destroy the idol itself. Instead God punishes the people and leaves the idol standing. The philosopher wants to know why.

keyTerms.meaning: A philosopher, a non-Jewish thinker
A jealous God, one who does not tolerate rivals
Is jealous, takes action against

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאַל פִלוֹסֹפוּס אֶחָד אֶת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל:
phrases.english: A certain philosopher asked Rabban Gamliel:
It is written in your Torah:
"For ה׳ your God is a consuming fire,

phrases.notes: דברים 4:24

phrases.english: Why is He jealous of its worshippers
but not jealous of it itself?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל פִלוֹסֹפוּס אֶחָד אֶת רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל

steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why God punishes idol worshippers but does not destroy the idol itself

steps.title: רבן גמליאל's parable of the king, his son and the dog
steps.stepSummary: A king's son names his dog after his father and swears by 'the life of the dog, my father'. The king is angry at the son, not at the dog.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I will give you a parable. What is this like? It is like a human king who had one son. That son raised a dog and gave it his father's name. When he swore, he would say, 'By the life of the dog, my father.' When the king heard this, who was he angry at, the son or the dog? You must say he was angry at the son.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל answers the philosopher with a parable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dog did nothing wrong. It is the son who insulted his father by giving the father's honor to a dog. In the same way, the idol is just an object. The guilt belongs to the people who treat it as a god, so God's anger is aimed at them.

keyTerms.meaning: A parable, a story used as a comparison
What is this like? It opens a parable
A human king, literally 'a king of flesh and blood'
You must say; the answer is obvious

phrases.english: He said to him: I will give you a parable.
What is this like?

phrases.english: It is like a human king who had one son,

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹתוֹ הַבֵּן הָיָה מְגַדֵּל לוֹ אֶת הַכֶּלֶב

phrases.english: and gave it a name after his father's name,
and when he swore he would say: "By the life of the dog, my father."

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֶׁשָּׁמַע הַמֶּלֶךְ, עַל מִי הוּא כּוֹעֵס,
phrases.english: When the king heard, who is he angry at?
Is he angry at the son
or is he angry at the dog?

phrases.aramaic: הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: עַל הַבֵּן הוּא כּוֹעֵס.
phrases.english: You must say: he is angry at the son.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the philosopher's question from step 25
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The idol is like a dog that someone wrongly honors. The blame and the anger fall on the person who gives it God's honor, not on the object.

steps.title: The philosopher objects that the idol has real power
steps.stepSummary: The philosopher rejects the comparison to a dog and claims the idol has real substance and power.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You call it a dog? But it has real power!
steps.whatsHappening: The philosopher pushes back against רבן גמליאל's parable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The parable only works if the idol is worthless like a dog. The philosopher attacks exactly that point and claims the idol truly has power.

keyTerms.meaning: Real substance or power
But surely; it opens a challenge

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: כֶּלֶב אַתָּה קוֹרֵא אוֹתָהּ?
phrases.english: He said to him: You call it a dog?
But it has real power!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: כֶּלֶב אַתָּה קוֹרֵא אוֹתָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the main assumption of the parable in step 26
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן גמליאל's comparison of the idol to a powerless dog
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the idol has real power, it is not like a dog, and the parable falls apart.

steps.title: רבן גמליאל asks what he saw
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל asks the philosopher what evidence makes him think the idol has power.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: And what did you see?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל asks for proof. This short question sets up the philosopher's story in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of arguing, רבן גמליאל asks what the claim is based on. This draws out the evidence so it can be dealt with.

keyTerms.meaning: And what did you see? What is your evidence?

phrases.english: He said to him: And what did you see?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: וּמָה רָאִיתָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the basis of the objection in step 27
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What evidence shows the idol has power

steps.title: The philosopher's proof: the fire that spared the idol's temple
steps.stepSummary: The philosopher reports that a fire burned his whole city but did not burn the idol's temple.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Once a fire broke out in our city, and the whole city burned down, but that temple of idol worship did not burn!
steps.whatsHappening: The philosopher brings his proof that the idol has power: a fire spared its temple.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He argues that the temple survived because the idol protected it. That would mean the idol is not a powerless 'dog'. רבן גמליאל answers this proof in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A fire
A temple of idol worship
Once

phrases.english: He said to him: Once
a fire broke out in our city,
and the entire city burned down,

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹתוֹ בֵּית עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לֹא נִשְׂרַף!
phrases.english: but that temple of idol worship did not burn!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: פַּעַם אַחַת נָפְלָה דְּלֵיקָה בְּעִירֵנוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 28 by giving evidence for the objection in step 27
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the idol has real power
steps.raayaSupportSource: A city fire that destroyed everything except the idol's temple

steps.title: A king fights the living, not the dead
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל answers the fire story with a parable. A king whose province rebels makes war on living people, not on the dead. So God's punishment goes to the living worshippers and not to the lifeless idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל said to him: Let me give you a parable. What is this like? It is like a human king whose province rebelled against him. When he goes to war, does he fight the living or the dead? Obviously, he fights the living.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל pushes back on the philosopher's proof that the idol's temple was spared because the idol has power. He gives a parable about a king at war.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The philosopher said the fire skipping the temple shows the idol is strong. רבן גמליאל flips this around. Punishment is aimed at living people who sinned, and the idol is like a dead thing that nobody bothers to fight. So the temple being spared proves nothing about the idol's power.

keyTerms.meaning: A parable, a comparison story
Flesh and blood: a human being, as opposed to God
Sinned, rebelled
A province or region
You must say: the answer is obvious

phrases.english: He said to him: I will tell you a parable,
what is the matter comparable to?
To a king of flesh and blood
whose province sinned against him.
When he wages war,
does he wage it against the living
or does he wage it against the dead?
phrases.notes: The "dead" stand for the idol, which has no life. The "living" are the people who worship it.

phrases.aramaic: הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: עִם הַחַיִּים הוּא עוֹשֶׂה.
phrases.english: You must say: he wages it against the living.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אֶמְשׁוֹל לְךָ מָשָׁל, לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the philosopher's fire proof from step 29.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof that the idol has power because its temple survived the fire.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Punishment is aimed at living sinners, not at a lifeless object. So the temple being spared says nothing about the idol's strength.

steps.title: Then why not destroy the idol?
steps.stepSummary: The philosopher argues that if the idol is just a dog or a dead thing, God should get rid of it completely.
steps.simpleTranslation: The philosopher said to him: You call the idol a dog, and you call it dead. If so, let God remove it from the world!
steps.whatsHappening: The philosopher challenges רבן גמליאל using his own two parables. If the idol is worthless, why does God leave it in the world?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן גמליאל compared the idol to a dog (step 26) and to the dead (step 30). The philosopher says this proves too much. Something that worthless, which still causes people to sin, should simply be wiped out.

keyTerms.meaning: A dog
He should destroy it, wipe it out

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: כֶּלֶב אַתָּה קוֹרֵא אוֹתָהּ,
phrases.english: He said to him: You call it a dog,
phrases.notes: This points back to the parable of the king's son who named his dog after his father (step 26).

phrases.english: you call it dead;
if so, let Him remove it from the world!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: כֶּלֶב אַתָּה קוֹרֵא אוֹתָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבן גמליאל's parables from steps 26 and 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן גמליאל's claim that the idol is worthless, like a dog or a dead thing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the idol is truly worthless, God has no reason to keep it around. He should destroy it.

steps.title: God won't destroy the world because of fools
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל explains that people also worship the sun, moon, stars, constellations, streams and valleys. God will not destroy these things, which the world needs, just because foolish people worship them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן גמליאל said to him: If people worshipped only things the world does not need, God would get rid of them. But they worship the sun and the moon, the stars and the constellations, the streams and the valleys. Should God destroy His world because of fools?
steps.whatsHappening: רבן גמליאל answers the philosopher's challenge. He explains why God does not wipe out what people worship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees that God would destroy a useless object of worship. But many objects of worship are basic parts of creation that the world needs. Destroying them would mean destroying the world, and God will not do that because some people act foolishly.

keyTerms.meaning: He would get rid of it
The sun and the moon
Constellations
Streams and valleys
Fools

steps.whatToRemember: God punishes the people who worship idols, not the objects they worship. Many of those objects, like the sun and moon, are things the world needs, so God leaves them in place.

phrases.english: He said to him: If it were an object

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין הָעוֹלָם צָרִיךְ לוֹ הָיוּ עוֹבְדִין,
phrases.english: that the world has no need for that they worshipped,
He would eliminate it.
But they worship the sun and the moon,
the stars and the constellations,
the streams and the valleys.
Should He destroy His world because of fools?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: אִילּוּ לְדָבָר שֶׁאֵין הָעוֹלָם צָרִיךְ לוֹ הָיוּ עוֹבְדִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the philosopher's challenge from step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the principle: God destroys useless objects of worship, but not things the world needs.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since an idol is worthless, God should destroy every object of worship.
steps.terutzMaskana: Many objects of worship are needed for the world to exist, so God leaves them and punishes only the worshippers.

steps.title: Introducing a supporting verse
steps.stepSummary: רבן גמליאל begins to bring a פסוק that supports his answer. The פסוק itself comes in the next part of the text.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so the verse says:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. רבן גמליאל is about to quote a פסוק to back up what he just said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'and so it says' tell us a source is coming to support the idea that God does not destroy His world because of idol worshippers. The actual פסוק appears in the next lines of the גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: And so it says: the opening for a supporting פסוק

phrases.english: And so it says:

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Prepares a supporting פסוק for the answer in step 32.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that God does not destroy His world because of fools who worship parts of it.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A פסוק quoted in the next lines of the גמרא.
